Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning

Jinyu Zhang Affiliation: School of Transportation, Southeast University, Nanjing, China Affiliation: Urban Transport Systems Laboratory (LUTS)École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland*Corresponding author    Di Huang Affiliation: School of Transportation, Southeast University, Nanjing, China    Zhiyuan Liu Affiliation: School of Transportation, Southeast University, Nanjing, China Affiliation: School of Statistics and Data Science, Southeast University, Nanjing, China    Nikolas Geroliminis Affiliation: Urban Transport Systems Laboratory (LUTS)École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland*Corresponding author
Abstract

Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply–demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector–Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

Keywords: ride-hailing; vehicle repositioning; macroscopic fundamental diagram; multistage contextual optimization.

1 Introduction

Ride-hailing demand varies across space and time, while the vehicle distribution reflects earlier trips. Vehicles may remain idle in one region as requests wait in another (Zhang et al. 2023). Repositioning can correct this imbalance, but it incurs an immediate empty-trip cost and removes a vehicle from service until it arrives (Pavone et al. 2012, Pantelidis et al. 2022). The problem is therefore prediction-driven and multistage. At each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current repositioning and service under the available information, and updates the fleet state. The resulting idle and in-motion stocks become the initial state for the next stage.

Repositioning and service also interact with congestion across the city. Empty repositioning, occupied trips, and vehicles already in motion all contribute to regional accumulation (Xu et al. 2021). Near the production-maximizing regime, an additional trip consumes scarce road capacity and delays vehicle return. We argue that in systems with a large number of ride-hailing vehicles (as in many large cities worldwide), vehicle repositioning can influence the level of congestion and regional speeds in different parts of the network. The macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) describes this effect at the same regional level at which repositioning is decided: it represents an aggregate, robust, and empirically validated relation between vehicle accumulation and production or speed (Geroliminis and Daganzo 2008, Paipuri et al. 2021). The MFD has recently been integrated into dynamic ride-sourcing models (Ramezani and Valadkhani 2023, Beojone and Geroliminis 2023) and vehicle-repositioning methods (Valadkhani and Ramezani 2023, Beojone et al. 2024, Huang et al. 2024b) to capture congestion feedback.

Ride-hailing demand predictors are usually trained for forecast accuracy, such as OD-level spatio-temporal deep learning models (Ke et al. 2021). However, the cost of a forecast error depends on where idle vehicles are, and their locations depend on earlier repositioning and trips. Contextual optimization addresses this mismatch: it predicts uncertain parameters for a downstream optimization model and trains the predictor on decision performance rather than numerical forecast error (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020, Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022, Huang et al. 2024a, Huang et al. 2025). Methodological extensions handle uncertain constraints (Hu et al. 2023), decision-dependent uncertainty (Liu et al. 2022), and multistage problems (Hu et al. 2024, Peršak and Anjos 2025). The two multistage studies propagate gradients across stages, but neither captures how the inherited state changes the forecast as context, and Peršak and Anjos (2025) restrict uncertainty to the objective. In transportation, recent studies apply contextual optimization to vehicle repositioning and show that decision-based training can improve downstream performance (Guo et al. 2026, Wang et al. 2026). However, they treat vehicle repositioning as a single optimization stage, so they cannot capture how current decisions change the state and operating cost of later stages.

Existing studies therefore leave a gap between MFD-aware repositioning and contextual optimization. MFD-aware repositioning takes demand forecasts as given, and contextual optimization has not been developed for a multistage policy in which the forecast sets the current decisions, these decisions change the next state, and this state is again an input of the predictor. Closing this gap raises three challenges. First, demand often enters operating constraints, so decisions computed from forecasts must remain feasible when current demand is realized. Second, each inherited state enters both the predictor and the operational model, so gradients must propagate through both paths and the recursive state trajectory; without the path through the predictor, the gradient misses how the parameters change later forecasts. Third, training repeatedly solves optimization models across many stages. Existing acceleration methods reduce the cost of differentiation (Amos and Kolter 2017, Berthet et al. 2020) or the number of solver calls (Mulamba et al. 2021), and Hu et al. (2024) update per-stage networks in parallel, but none of them shortens the sequential forward evaluation of one sample, which remains the bottleneck of training.

To close this gap, this paper makes three contributions. First, we formulate MFD-aware multistage vehicle repositioning as a rolling commitment–recourse policy. It separates pre-realization repositioning from post-realization service. We linearize the MFD dynamics and penalize an upper bound on the resulting movement error. Second, we develop a multistage contextual optimization approach in which the predictor uses the decision-induced operating state as context. Our problem involves coupled stages, decision-dependent context, and forecasts that change the objective, constraint matrix, and right-hand sides (RHS) of every stage linear program (LP). For this problem, we derive the exact gradient of the complete multistage graph, together with an equivalent adjoint that avoids full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Third, we propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of stages in parallel to accelerate training. We prove that it recovers the serial trajectory within finitely many passes and that its gradient error stays bounded under early stopping.

2 MFD-Aware Rolling-Horizon Repositioning Model

This section constructs an MFD-aware vehicle-repositioning model. We first describe the problem setting (Section 2.1) and formulate the multi-period planning problem (Section 2.2). We then derive an affine approximation of its traffic dynamics (Section 2.3) and describe multistage execution (Section 2.4). Finally, we make decisions under forecast demand with a commitment–recourse scheme (Section 2.5) and update its reference trajectory (Section 2.6).

2.1 Problem Setting

We study an urban ride-hailing platform that operates across service regions. At each decision stage, its operating state consists of idle vehicles, waiting requests, and vehicles in motion. It forecasts future regional demand and proactively repositions part of the idle fleet toward regions expected to face high demand. This action can improve the future supply–demand balance, but it incurs empty-travel cost. The platform therefore coordinates service and repositioning over time to limit the waiting-request backlog, request abandonment, and empty travel. Repositioning also changes the traffic state. Idle, occupied, and empty in-motion platform vehicles contribute to regional accumulation together with background traffic. At high accumulation, a further increase can reduce production and delay vehicle return. We represent this feedback with a regional MFD. The model thus captures both effects of repositioning: it changes the future supply distribution and the congestion under which that supply becomes available. Figure 1 illustrates both effects in three regions.

At each decision stage, the platform makes two linked decisions under different information. It first uses the current operating state and a rolling demand forecast to commit part of the idle fleet to repositioning. The remaining idle vehicles stay available for passenger service. After current requests are observed, the platform decides how to serve new and waiting requests subject to the earlier repositioning commitment. Repositioning and service change vehicle locations and the waiting-request backlog, while MFD dynamics determine vehicle movement. The state reached after the current period initializes the next stage. The problem is multistage because current actions affect later operating states and hence the decisions made there.

2.2 Multi-Period Repositioning Model

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the region set and ℰ⊆ℛ×ℛ\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{R} the directed edge set connecting adjacent regions. The planning horizon contains H≥1H\geq 1 periods of length Δ>0\Delta>0, where HH is an integer, indexed by ℋ={0,…,H−1}\mathcal{H}=\{0,\ldots,H-1\}. Let 𝒟pax=ℛ×ℛ\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}=\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{R} be the passenger origin–destination (OD) set. Repositioning uses its off-diagonal subset 𝒟off:={(i,j)∈𝒟pax:i≠j}\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}:=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}:i\neq j\}. Movement classes

The platform can send a vehicle through the network in three ways. An idle vehicle can carry a passenger directly from an origin to a destination. It can instead travel empty toward a target destination as a repositioning action. During this empty trip, it may also pick up a passenger in an intermediate region and carry that passenger to the same target destination (Figure 1). This loaded pickup conversion uses the same off-diagonal OD set 𝒟off\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}. Here oo is the original origin of an empty itinerary, while ii is a passenger pickup origin. For each (i,j)∈𝒟pax(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}, let 𝒫i​j=(p0i​j=i,p1i​j,…,pLi​ji​j=j)\mathcal{P}_{ij}=(p^{ij}_{0}=i,p^{ij}_{1},\ldots,p^{ij}_{L_{ij}}=j) be a fixed directed path whose consecutive regions are adjacent in ℰ\mathcal{E}. Demand backlog and abandonment

Let KwaitK^{\mathrm{wait}} be the nonnegative integer number of additional periods for which a request remains available after its arrival period. For service period τ\tau, define the admissible arrival-period set 𝒯τarr:={τ−Kwait,…,τ}\mathcal{T}_{\tau}^{\mathrm{arr}}:=\{\tau-K^{\mathrm{wait}},\ldots,\tau\}. For τ′∈𝒯τarr\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{\tau}^{\mathrm{arr}}, let qi​j,τ,τ′q_{ij,\tau,\tau^{\prime}} be the corresponding request stock available before service. Requests of one OD pair that arrived in the same period τ′\tau^{\prime} form an arrival cohort. The current cohort holds the new requests, qi​j,τ,τ=di​j,τq_{ij,\tau,\tau}=d_{ij,\tau}. Ordinary service and pickup conversion can serve cohorts with τ′∈𝒯τarr\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{\tau}^{\mathrm{arr}}. Let μi​j,τ,τ′\mu_{ij,\tau,\tau^{\prime}} be the service assigned to the cohort from τ′\tau^{\prime}, and let μi​j,τ\mu_{ij,\tau} be the total volume served. Summing the cohort allocations must equal the passenger-service flow supplied by ordinary dispatch and pickup conversion:

μi​j,τ:=∑τ′∈𝒯τarrμi​j,τ,τ′=mi​j,τ+∑o:(o,j)∈𝒟off,i∈𝒫o​j∖{o,j}yo​i​j,τ,∀(i,j)∈𝒟pax,τ∈ℋ.\mu_{ij,\tau}:=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{\tau}^{\mathrm{arr}}}\mu_{ij,\tau,\tau^{\prime}}=m_{ij,\tau}+\sum_{o:\,(o,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}},\ i\in\mathcal{P}_{oj}\setminus\{o,j\}}y_{oij,\tau},\qquad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}. (2.7)

MFD dynamics

The end-of-period state transition is

Objective

Let cq≥0c^{q}\geq 0 and cA≥0c^{A}\geq 0 be the penalties per waiting request-period and per abandoned request, common to all OD pairs. The cost co​jg≥0c^{g}_{oj}\geq 0 applies to each vehicle committed to repositioning on (o,j)∈𝒟off(o,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}. The reward bi​j≥0b_{ij}\geq 0 applies to each completed passenger trip on (i,j)∈𝒟pax(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}, whether through ordinary service or pickup conversion. The planning-horizon objective JplanJ^{\mathrm{plan}} is

Jplan=∑τ=0H−1[∑(i,j)∈𝒟paxcqqi​j,τ+1+∑(i,j)∈𝒟paxcAAi​j,τ+∑(o,j)∈𝒟offcgo​jgo​j,τ\displaystyle J^{\mathrm{plan}}=\sum_{\tau=0}^{H-1}\left[\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}}c^{q}q_{ij,\tau+1}+\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}}c^{A}A_{ij,\tau}+\sum_{(o,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}}c^{g}_{oj}g_{oj,\tau}\right. (2.19)
−∑(i,j)∈𝒟paxbi​jC¯ai​jsrvj,τ−∑(i,j)∈𝒟offbi​jC¯ai​jloadj,τ].\displaystyle\left.-\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}}b_{ij}\bar{C}^{a_{ij}^{\mathrm{srv}}}_{j,\tau}-\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}}b_{ij}\bar{C}^{a_{ij}^{\mathrm{load}}}_{j,\tau}\right].

The planning horizon ends after period H−1H-1. Passengers still on board at that time complete their trips after the horizon, so (2.19) gives these trips no reward, and the plan may undervalue pickups late in the horizon. As in the terminal cost of finite-horizon dynamic programming, we approximate this cost-to-go by crediting occupied in-motion vehicles at the end of the horizon, whose rewards no longer depend on later decisions or demand:

Jterm=−ν∑a∈𝒜srv∪𝒜load∑k∈ℛb𝗈⁡(a)​𝖽​(a)nak,H,J^{\mathrm{term}}=-\nu\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{srv}}\cup\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{load}}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{R}}b_{\mathsf{o}(a)\mathsf{d}(a)}\,n^{a}_{k,H}, (2.20)

where ν≥0\nu\geq 0 is the credit fraction. The continuous-time MFD planning problem is

minm,g,y,μ,A,ι,e~,n~,n¯,e,q,n,N,M,C,M¯,C¯Jplan+Jterm\displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,g,y,\mu,A,\iota,\tilde{e},\\ \tilde{n},\bar{n},e,q,n,N,M,C,\bar{M},\bar{C}\end{subarray}}\quad J^{\mathrm{plan}}+J^{\mathrm{term}} (2.21)

subject to the dispatch and pickup constraints (2.1)–(2.6), demand constraints (2.7)–(2.10) with the current cohort and initial state, and MFD dynamics and state balances (2.11)–(2.18). Although vehicles and requests are discrete, we use a continuous relaxation of the allocation and state variables for regional planning. All decision variables are continuous and nonnegative.

2.3 Affine MFD Approximation

The model above links repositioning to future vehicle availability through continuous traffic dynamics. Solving it requires tracking stocks and flows within every decision period, while the MFD makes movement rates nonlinear in class stocks and regional accumulation. These features complicate the multi-period optimization. We therefore discretize the traffic dynamics and approximate the nonlinear movement equations by affine relations, yielding an LP for horizon planning.

Forward Euler Discretization

We first approximate traffic evolution with one forward Euler step of length Δ\Delta per period. Movement rates are evaluated at the period’s initial state, after dispatch and pickup conversion. The available moving and idle stocks are therefore n¯k,τa\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau} and e~k,τ\tilde{e}_{k,\tau}. Let Nk,τbg=Nk,τbg​(0)N^{\mathrm{bg}}_{k,\tau}=N^{\mathrm{bg}}_{k,\tau}(0) denote the given background accumulation at the start of the period. Total accumulation can be written as

Nk,τ=Nk,τbg+e~k,τ+∑a∈𝒜n¯k,τa,0≤Nk,τ≤Nkjam,∀k∈ℛ,τ∈ℋ.N_{k,\tau}=N^{\mathrm{bg}}_{k,\tau}+\tilde{e}_{k,\tau}+\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau},\qquad 0\leq N_{k,\tau}\leq N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}},\quad\forall k\in\mathcal{R},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}. (2.22)

The MFD rates in (2.14)–(2.15) give the following period movement fraction under the Euler approximation:

φk​(N)=Δ​Pk​(N)ℓ¯k​N,∀k∈ℛ,0<N≤Nkjam.\varphi_{k}(N)=\frac{\Delta P_{k}(N)}{\bar{\ell}_{k}N},\qquad\forall k\in\mathcal{R},\quad 0<N\leq N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}}. (2.23)

At N=0N=0, φk\varphi_{k} is defined by continuity. Applying this fraction to the available class stock gives the period movement volume

fk,τa=n¯k,τa​φk​(Nk,τ),∀a∈𝒜,k∈ℛ,τ∈ℋ.f^{a}_{k,\tau}=\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}\varphi_{k}(N_{k,\tau}),\qquad\forall a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{R},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}. (2.24)

We choose a sufficiently small period length Δ>0\Delta>0 so that 0≤φk​(N)<10\leq\varphi_{k}(N)<1 for every region and all N∈[0,Nkjam]N\in[0,N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}}]. This keeps period outflow within the available stock. Using the path indicators in (2.13), the Euler approximations of the integrated flows in (2.17) are

M¯k​k′,τa\displaystyle\bar{M}^{a}_{kk^{\prime},\tau} =χk​k′𝗈⁡(a)​𝖽​(a),edge​fk,τa,\displaystyle=\chi^{\mathsf{o}(a)\mathsf{d}(a),\mathrm{edge}}_{kk^{\prime}}f^{a}_{k,\tau}, ∀(k,k′)∈ℰ,a∈𝒜,τ∈ℋ,\displaystyle\forall(k,k^{\prime})\in\mathcal{E},\ a\in\mathcal{A},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}, (2.25)
C¯k,τa\displaystyle\bar{C}^{a}_{k,\tau} =χk𝗈⁡(a)​𝖽​(a),term​fk,τa,\displaystyle=\chi^{\mathsf{o}(a)\mathsf{d}(a),\mathrm{term}}_{k}f^{a}_{k,\tau}, ∀k∈ℛ,a∈𝒜,τ∈ℋ.\displaystyle\forall k\in\mathcal{R},\ a\in\mathcal{A},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}.

With these flows, the period balances (2.18) replace the continuous evolution in (2.16).

Affine movement equations

The period balances are linear, but the movement volume (2.24) still depends nonlinearly on class stock and regional accumulation. In the first period, dispatch and pickup conversion preserve total regional stock, so Nk,0N_{k,0} is fixed by the initial state and fk,0a=φk​(Nk,0)​n¯k,0af^{a}_{k,0}=\varphi_{k}(N_{k,0})\,\bar{n}^{a}_{k,0} is already linear. For later periods, we use a first-order expansion around a reference trajectory 𝒏=(n¯ref,Nref)\bm{n}=(\bar{n}^{\mathrm{ref}},N^{\mathrm{ref}}), where n¯k,τa,ref\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau} and Nk,τrefN^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau} are the reference post-conversion class stock and total regional accumulation, respectively:

fk,τa\displaystyle f^{a}_{k,\tau} =n¯k,τa,ref​φk​(Nk,τref)+φk​(Nk,τref)​(n¯k,τa−n¯k,τa,ref)+n¯k,τa,ref​φk′​(Nk,τref)​(Nk,τ−Nk,τref)\displaystyle=\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\varphi_{k}(N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})+\varphi_{k}(N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})(\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}-\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})+\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\varphi^{\prime}_{k}(N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})(N_{k,\tau}-N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}) (2.26)
=φk​(Nk,τref)​n¯k,τa⏟stock effect+n¯k,τa,ref​φk′​(Nk,τref)​(Nk,τ−Nk,τref)⏟congestion effect,∀a∈𝒜,k∈ℛ,τ∈ℋ∖{0}.\displaystyle=\underbrace{\varphi_{k}(N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}}_{\text{stock effect}}+\underbrace{\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\varphi^{\prime}_{k}(N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})(N_{k,\tau}-N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})}_{\text{congestion effect}},\quad\forall a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{R},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}\setminus\{0\}.

Section 2.6 describes how this trajectory is constructed. All coefficients are evaluated before the LP is solved. We also impose the physical bounds

0≤fk,τa≤n¯k,τa,∀a∈𝒜,k∈ℛ,τ∈ℋ.0\leq f^{a}_{k,\tau}\leq\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau},\qquad\forall a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{R},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}. (2.27)

Approximation-error control

The affine relation matches movement at the reference, but its error can grow as planned stocks and accumulation move away from that trajectory. We seek to penalize this movement error. Its exact absolute value contains the nonlinear product n¯k,τa​φk​(Nk,τ)\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}\varphi_{k}(N_{k,\tau}), so including it directly in the objective would lose the LP structure. We first bound the error by a weighted sum of squared stock and accumulation deviations.

Proposition 2.1 (Affine movement error bound).

Suppose φk\varphi_{k} is twice continuously differentiable on [0,Nkjam][0,N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}}], with |φk′|≤φ¯k′|\varphi^{\prime}_{k}|\leq\bar{\varphi}^{\prime}_{k} and |φk′′|≤φ¯k′′|\varphi^{\prime\prime}_{k}|\leq\bar{\varphi}^{\prime\prime}_{k} for constants φ¯k′,φ¯k′′≥0\bar{\varphi}^{\prime}_{k},\bar{\varphi}^{\prime\prime}_{k}\geq 0. The error satisfies

|n¯k,τa​φk​(Nk,τ)−fk,τa|≤φ¯k′2​(n¯k,τa−n¯k,τa,ref)2+φ¯k′+n¯k,τa,ref​φ¯k′′2​(Nk,τ−Nk,τref)2,∀a∈𝒜,k∈𝒫𝗈⁡(a),𝖽⁡(a),τ∈ℋ∖{0}.\begin{gathered}\left|\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}\varphi_{k}(N_{k,\tau})-f^{a}_{k,\tau}\right|\leq\frac{\bar{\varphi}^{\prime}_{k}}{2}\left(\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}-\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\right)^{2}+\frac{\bar{\varphi}^{\prime}_{k}+\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\bar{\varphi}^{\prime\prime}_{k}}{2}\left(N_{k,\tau}-N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\right)^{2},\\ \forall a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{o}(a),\mathsf{d}(a)},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}\setminus\{0\}.\end{gathered} (2.28)

Appendix A proves this bound. Directly penalizing the squared deviations would give a quadratic objective. To keep the planning problem linear, we replace each square by a convex piecewise-linear upper envelope. Let δ\delta denote either the stock deviation n¯k,τa−n¯k,τa,ref\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}-\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau} or the accumulation deviation Nk,τ−Nk,τrefN_{k,\tau}-N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}. Choose S+1S+1 fixed points (ξh,ξh2)(\xi_{h},\xi_{h}^{2}) on the curve δ2\delta^{2}, where the integer S≥2S\geq 2 is the number of segments and ξ0<⋯<ξS\xi_{0}<\cdots<\xi_{S}. Set the endpoints to ξ0=−maxk∈ℛ⁡Nkjam\xi_{0}=-\max_{k\in\mathcal{R}}N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}} and ξS=maxk∈ℛ⁡Nkjam\xi_{S}=\max_{k\in\mathcal{R}}N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}}, and include (0,0)(0,0) among the points. Connecting adjacent points defines the envelope Ψ\Psi. Each segment has slope γh\gamma_{h} and intercept βh\beta_{h}:

Ψ(δ)=(ξh+ξh+1)⏟γhδ+(−ξh​ξh+1)⏟βh,∀δ∈[ξh,ξh+1],h∈{0,…,S−1}.\displaystyle\Psi(\delta)=\underbrace{(\xi_{h}+\xi_{h+1})}_{\gamma_{h}}\delta+\underbrace{(-\xi_{h}\xi_{h+1})}_{\beta_{h}},\qquad\forall\delta\in[\xi_{h},\xi_{h+1}],\ h\in\{0,\ldots,S-1\}. (2.29)

Since Ψ\Psi is a maximum of finitely many affine functions, we represent the stock and accumulation envelopes by auxiliary variables ψk,τa,stk\psi^{a,\mathrm{stk}}_{k,\tau} and ψk,τacc\psi^{\mathrm{acc}}_{k,\tau} with linear constraints

ψk,τa,stk\displaystyle\psi^{a,\mathrm{stk}}_{k,\tau} ≥γh(n¯ak,τ−n¯a,refk,τ)+βh,∀a∈𝒜,k∈𝒫𝗈⁡(a),𝖽⁡(a),h∈{0,…,S−1},τ∈ℋ∖{0},\displaystyle\geq\gamma_{h}(\bar{n}^{a}_{k,\tau}-\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})+\beta_{h},\forall a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{o}(a),\mathsf{d}(a)},\ h\in\{0,\ldots,S-1\},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}\setminus\{0\}, (2.30)
ψk,τacc\displaystyle\psi^{\mathrm{acc}}_{k,\tau} ≥γh(Nk,τ−Nrefk,τ)+βh,∀k∈ℛ,h∈{0,…,S−1},τ∈ℋ∖{0}.\displaystyle\geq\gamma_{h}(N_{k,\tau}-N^{\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau})+\beta_{h},\forall k\in\mathcal{R},\ h\in\{0,\ldots,S-1\},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}\setminus\{0\}.

The coefficients in (2.28) are nonnegative, so replacing the squares by these variables preserves the upper bound on movement error. This gives the penalty

R^ak,τ:=φ¯k′2ψa,stkk,τ+φ¯k′+n¯k,τa,ref​φ¯k′′2ψacck,τ,∀a∈𝒜,k∈𝒫𝗈⁡(a),𝖽⁡(a),τ∈ℋ∖{0}.\begin{gathered}\widehat{R}^{a}_{k,\tau}:=\frac{\bar{\varphi}^{\prime}_{k}}{2}\psi^{a,\mathrm{stk}}_{k,\tau}+\frac{\bar{\varphi}^{\prime}_{k}+\bar{n}^{a,\mathrm{ref}}_{k,\tau}\bar{\varphi}^{\prime\prime}_{k}}{2}\psi^{\mathrm{acc}}_{k,\tau},\qquad\forall a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{o}(a),\mathsf{d}(a)},\ \tau\in\mathcal{H}\setminus\{0\}.\end{gathered} (2.31)

The penalty R^\widehat{R} is the mean of R^k,τa\widehat{R}^{a}_{k,\tau} over all index combinations in (2.31). With weight cmfd>0c^{\mathrm{mfd}}>0, initial state ss, demand dd, and reference 𝒏\bm{n}, the planning LP is

minm,g,y,μ,A,ι,e~,n~,n¯,e,q,n,N,f,M¯,C¯,ψstk,ψaccJplan+Jterm+cmfd​R^,\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,g,y,\mu,A,\iota,\tilde{e},\tilde{n},\bar{n},\\ e,q,n,N,f,\bar{M},\bar{C},\psi^{\mathrm{stk}},\psi^{\mathrm{acc}}\end{subarray}}\quad J^{\mathrm{plan}}+J^{\mathrm{term}}+c^{\mathrm{mfd}}\widehat{R}, (2.32)

subject to the dispatch and pickup constraints (2.1)–(2.6), demand constraints (2.7)–(2.10) with the current cohort and initial state, accumulation bounds (2.22), path flows (2.25), state balances (2.18), movement equations and stock bounds (2.26)–(2.27), and penalty constraints (2.30). Stocks and flows outside class paths are zero, and all variables are continuous and nonnegative.

When platform traffic penetration is low, dispatch decisions may have little effect on regional speeds. Speeds can then be treated as exogenous, so a fixed fraction min⁡{1,Δ​vk,τ/ℓ¯k}\min\{1,\Delta v_{k,\tau}/\bar{\ell}_{k}\} of each class stock in region kk moves on during period τ\tau, where vk,τv_{k,\tau} is the exogenous regional speed. These fixed-fraction movements replace the accumulation and movement equations and the penalty in (2.32), which gives the fixed-fraction LP.

2.4 Multistage Repositioning

We link successive LP horizons through their first-period end states. Let 𝒯={0,…,T−1}\mathcal{T}=\{0,\ldots,T-1\} index the T≥1T\geq 1 decision stages. At stage t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, t+ℓ|tt+\ell\mid t denotes period t+ℓt+\ell planned at stage tt, with lead ℓ∈ℋ\ell\in\mathcal{H}. Thus LP period τ∈ℋ\tau\in\mathcal{H} of the stage-tt problem is absolute period t+τt+\tau. The horizon demand vector dt:t+H−1|td_{t:t+H-1\mid t} stacks these periods’ OD demand inputs. The multistage procedure starts from s0=(e0,q0,n0)s_{0}=(e^{0},q^{0},n^{0}):

ei,0|0\displaystyle e_{i,0\mid 0} =ei0,\displaystyle=e_{i}^{0}, ∀i∈ℛ,\displaystyle\forall i\in\mathcal{R}, (2.33)
qi​j,0,τ′|0\displaystyle q_{ij,0,\tau^{\prime}\mid 0} =qi​j,0,τ′0,\displaystyle=q_{ij,0,\tau^{\prime}}^{0}, ∀(i,j)∈𝒟pax,τ′∈𝒯0arr∖{0},\displaystyle\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}},\ \tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{0}^{\mathrm{arr}}\setminus\{0\},
nk,0|0a\displaystyle n^{a}_{k,0\mid 0} =nka,0,\displaystyle=n_{k}^{a,0}, ∀k∈ℛ,a∈𝒜.\displaystyle\forall k\in\mathcal{R},\ a\in\mathcal{A}.

At each stage t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, solve (2.32) from sts_{t} with horizon demand dt:t+H−1|td_{t:t+H-1\mid t} and a given reference trajectory. Let uu collect its decision variables and ut⋆u_{t}^{\star} denote an optimal plan. Only current-period actions are executed. Let ztz_{t} collect these service, repositioning, and pickup decisions together with the first-period backlog, abandonment, and trip completions used to evaluate cost. Let Πz\Pi_{z} be their fixed selector:

zt=Πz​ut⋆,∀t∈𝒯.z_{t}=\Pi_{z}u_{t}^{\star},\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}. (2.34)

The first-period end state in this optimal plan directly initializes the next planning horizon:

ei,t+1|t+1\displaystyle e_{i,t+1\mid t+1} =ei,t+1|t⋆,\displaystyle=e^{\star}_{i,t+1\mid t}, ∀i∈ℛ,t∈𝒯∖{T−1},\displaystyle\forall i\in\mathcal{R},\ t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{T-1\}, (2.35)
qi​j,t+1,τ′|t+1\displaystyle q_{ij,t+1,\tau^{\prime}\mid t+1} =qi​j,t+1,τ′|t⋆,\displaystyle=q^{\star}_{ij,t+1,\tau^{\prime}\mid t}, ∀(i,j)∈𝒟pax,τ′∈𝒯t+1arr∖{t+1},t∈𝒯∖{T−1},\displaystyle\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}},\ \tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{arr}}\setminus\{t+1\},\ t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{T-1\},
nk,t+1|t+1a\displaystyle n^{a}_{k,t+1\mid t+1} =nk,t+1|ta,⋆,\displaystyle=n^{a,\star}_{k,t+1\mid t}, ∀k∈ℛ,a∈𝒜,t∈𝒯∖{T−1}.\displaystyle\forall k\in\mathcal{R},\ a\in\mathcal{A},\ t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{T-1\}.

Let Πs\Pi_{s} select these stocks from the plan. Then st+1=Πs​ut⋆s_{t+1}=\Pi_{s}u_{t}^{\star} for all t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}. We evaluate each stage by the operating cost of its executed decisions. The coefficient vector cc assigns the costs in (2.19) to the components of ztz_{t}:

Jtexec=c⊤​zt=\displaystyle J_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}=c^{\top}z_{t}={} cq​∑(i,j)∈𝒟paxqi​j,t+1|t⋆+cA​∑(i,j)∈𝒟paxAi​j,t|t⋆+∑(o,j)∈𝒟offco​jg​go​j,t|t⋆\displaystyle c^{q}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}}q^{\star}_{ij,t+1\mid t}+c^{A}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}}A^{\star}_{ij,t\mid t}+\sum_{(o,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}}c^{g}_{oj}g^{\star}_{oj,t\mid t} (2.36)
−∑(i,j)∈𝒟paxbi​jC¯ai​jsrv,⋆j,t|t−∑(i,j)∈𝒟offbi​jC¯ai​jload,⋆j,t|t,∀t∈𝒯.\displaystyle-\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}}b_{ij}\bar{C}^{a_{ij}^{\mathrm{srv}},\star}_{j,t\mid t}-\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{off}}}b_{ij}\bar{C}^{a_{ij}^{\mathrm{load}},\star}_{j,t\mid t},\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}.

The trajectory cost 𝒥\mathcal{J} is the sum of JtexecJ_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}} over all stages, so each executed period contributes once. Unlike the planning objective, 𝒥\mathcal{J} has no terminal cost. The trajectory covers the whole repositioning window of the day, so 𝒥\mathcal{J} is the realized operating cost of that window.

2.5 Commitment–Recourse with Demand Forecasts

The multistage procedure above takes horizon demand as a given input. This subsection replaces it with forecasts. In operation, demand is unknown when repositioning is committed, so the platform relies on forecasts d^i​j,t+ℓ|t\widehat{d}_{ij,t+\ell\mid t} for ℓ∈ℋ\ell\in\mathcal{H}. Simply substituting these forecasts for demand in the model can produce service decisions that exceed the requests actually available. A forecast-based current-period service plan satisfies μi​j,t|t≤∑τ′∈𝒯tarr∖{t}qi​j,t,τ′|t+d^i​j,t|t\mu_{ij,t\mid t}\leq\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t}^{\mathrm{arr}}\setminus\{t\}}q_{ij,t,\tau^{\prime}\mid t}+\widehat{d}_{ij,t\mid t} for each (i,j)∈𝒟pax(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}, whereas actual execution requires the same bound with the realized demand di​j,td_{ij,t} in place of the forecast. When the forecast exceeds realized demand, the plan can therefore serve more requests than are available. In practice, the platform first commits part of the idle fleet to repositioning and keeps the remaining vehicles available for service. It then chooses ordinary service and eligible pickup conversions under realized demand while retaining that commitment. We model this sequence with two linked LPs. The pre-realization LP uses forecast demand to choose the repositioning commitment. The post-realization LP uses realized current demand to choose service.

In the pre-realization commitment problem, let d^t\widehat{d}_{t} stack the nonnegative horizon forecast. Denote the solution map of (2.32) by LPtpre\mathrm{LP}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre}}. Let 𝒏tpre\bm{n}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre}} denote the pre reference vector at stage tt. The fixed selector Πg\Pi_{g} extracts the current repositioning commitment. The optimal plan and commitment are

utpre,⋆=LPtpre​(st,d^t,𝒏tpre),gtexec=Πg​utpre,⋆,∀t∈𝒯.u_{t}^{\mathrm{pre},\star}=\mathrm{LP}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre}}\!\left(s_{t},\widehat{d}_{t};\bm{n}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre}}\right),\qquad g_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}=\Pi_{g}u_{t}^{\mathrm{pre},\star},\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}. (2.37)

In the post-realization recourse problem, let dt=(di​j,t)(i,j)∈𝒟paxd_{t}=(d_{ij,t})_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}} collect realized current demand in the same OD order as each forecast block. Once dtd_{t} is observed, the post-realization problem uses it at lead zero and retains forecasts at later leads. Let the fixed selector Πfut\Pi_{\mathrm{fut}} remove lead zero, so d^tfut=Πfut​d^t\widehat{d}_{t}^{\mathrm{fut}}=\Pi_{\mathrm{fut}}\widehat{d}_{t} contains those later forecasts. Solve (2.32) from the same state sts_{t} with demand inputs (dt,d^tfut)(d_{t},\widehat{d}_{t}^{\mathrm{fut}}) and the fixed repositioning commitment go​j,t|tpost=go​j,texecg^{\mathrm{post}}_{oj,t\mid t}=g^{\mathrm{exec}}_{oj,t}. Denote this solution map by LPtpost\mathrm{LP}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}. Let 𝒏tpost\bm{n}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}} denote the corresponding post reference vector. Its optimal solution is

ůtpost=LPtpost​(st,dt,d^tfut,gtexec,𝒏tpost),∀t∈𝒯.\mathring{u}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}=\mathrm{LP}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}\!\left(s_{t},d_{t},\widehat{d}_{t}^{\mathrm{fut}},g_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}};\bm{n}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}\right),\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}. (2.38)

This solution provides current ordinary service, pickup, and cohort allocation. The LP decides how much of each arrival cohort to serve. Different splits of the same total service among cohorts can be equally optimal, so the cohort allocation may not be unique. We make it unique with a reallocation map 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}. The map keeps the LP’s total service and abandonment for each OD pair and period. Within these totals, it serves older cohorts first, after setting aside the requests that abandon at expiry. The map is piecewise affine and does not change the executed cost. Thus the post plan, executed decision, and next state are

utpost,⋆=𝒞t​(ůtpost),zt=Πz​utpost,⋆,st+1=Πs​utpost,⋆,∀t∈𝒯.u_{t}^{\mathrm{post},\star}=\mathcal{C}_{t}\bigl(\mathring{u}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}\bigr),\quad z_{t}=\Pi_{z}u_{t}^{\mathrm{post},\star},\quad s_{t+1}=\Pi_{s}u_{t}^{\mathrm{post},\star},\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}. (2.39)

The trajectory cost 𝒥\mathcal{J} then sums (2.36) over these ztz_{t}. This cost includes the repositioning commitment chosen by the pre problem and the service outcomes determined by the post problem. Figure 2 summarizes how this sequence links forecast-based repositioning to service under realized demand.

2.6 Reference-Trajectory Update

Both optimization layers require reference stocks and accumulations for (2.26). A reference whose stocks and accumulations differ substantially from those of the current problem may poorly represent congestion effects. Successive multistage problems have the same model structure and similar demand. Their optimal plans therefore provide useful decision preferences for constructing the references.

We first construct the post reference from the pre optimal plan at the same stage. The two problems differ only in current-period demand, which is forecasted in the pre problem and realized in the post problem. This difference alone prevents the pre optimum from serving directly as the post reference, because it may serve more requests than are available. We therefore keep the repositioning commitment and the pre plan’s allocation proportions, and propagate them through the traffic dynamics. A repair step scales service down to the available requests. Appendix B gives these steps and the references for the new tail period and the first stage. This construction defines the map

𝒏tpost=Reftpost⁡(st,dt,d^tfut,utpre,⋆),∀t∈𝒯.\bm{n}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}=\operatorname{Ref}_{t}^{\mathrm{post}}(s_{t},d_{t},\widehat{d}_{t}^{\mathrm{fut}},u_{t}^{\mathrm{pre},\star}),\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}. (2.40)

For each stage after initialization, we construct the pre reference from the preceding stage’s post optimal plan. The initial state also comes directly from that plan, and the two horizons share H−1H-1 periods. The plan still cannot be reused directly. Its decisions were made for the previous forecasts and may not fit the updated ones, and it has no decisions for the new final period. We therefore reuse the allocation shares (B.1) of the preceding post plan in the overlapping periods and carry its final-period shares into the tail. The same repair and propagation then give

𝒏tpre=Reftpre⁡(st,d^t,ut−1post,⋆),∀t∈𝒯∖{0}.\bm{n}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre}}=\operatorname{Ref}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre}}(s_{t},\widehat{d}_{t},u_{t-1}^{\mathrm{post},\star}),\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{0\}. (2.41)

At the first stage, no preceding plan is available. We solve the fixed-fraction LP of Section 2.3 under s0s_{0} and d^0\widehat{d}_{0}. Its optimal plan u0init,⋆u_{0}^{\mathrm{init},\star} supplies allocation proportions that account for future demand. The same repair and nonlinear propagation give

𝒏0pre=Refinit⁡(s0,d^0,u0init,⋆).\bm{n}_{0}^{\mathrm{pre}}=\operatorname{Ref}^{\mathrm{init}}(s_{0},\widehat{d}_{0},u_{0}^{\mathrm{init},\star}). (2.42)

Figure 3 summarizes the multistage policy.

3 Multistage Contextual Learning and Differentiation

The previous section defines a multistage commitment–recourse policy. We now train a demand predictor for this policy using operating cost together with prediction error. We first define the prediction architecture and computation graph (Section 3.1). We then differentiate the LP solutions (Section 3.2), combine them with the reference updates and state transitions into stage sensitivities (Section 3.3), and derive equivalent forward and adjoint gradients for training (Section 3.4).

3.1 Prediction Architecture and Computation Graph

We treat passenger demand as exogenous to platform operations and use decision-independent context xtexox_{t}^{\mathrm{exo}}, such as historical demand, to predict it. However, the operational effect of a forecast error depends on the state created by earlier decisions. For example, underpredicting ten requests may have little effect when an origin has ample idle vehicles, but may suppress needed vehicle inflows and increase backlog when supply is scarce. The predictor therefore uses xtexox_{t}^{\mathrm{exo}} together with the inherited operational state sts_{t}. A differentiable predictor maps both inputs to the demand vector d^t=fθ​(xtexo,st)∈ℝ+H​|𝒟pax|\widehat{d}_{t}=f_{\theta}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{exo}},s_{t})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{H|\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{pax}}|} for t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, where θ\theta is the trainable parameter vector of fθf_{\theta}. Appendix C specifies the prediction model. Let Ω\Omega be the set of training trajectories, each defined by an initial state and sequences of realized demand and exogenous context. For trajectory ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega, let ℓpred,tω​(d^t)\ell_{\mathrm{pred},t}^{\omega}(\widehat{d}_{t}) measure differentiable prediction error at stage t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}. The total prediction error is ℒpredω​(θ)=∑t∈𝒯ℓpred,tω​(d^t)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}^{\omega}(\theta)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\ell_{\mathrm{pred},t}^{\omega}(\widehat{d}_{t}). The trajectory cost of ω\omega is 𝒥ω​(θ)=∑t∈𝒯Jtexec,ω\mathcal{J}^{\omega}(\theta)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}J_{t}^{\mathrm{exec},\omega}. We train the predictor with the objective

ℒ⁡(θ)=1|Ω|​∑ω∈Ω∑t∈𝒯[Jtexec,ω⏟decision cost+α​ℓpred,tω​(d^t)⏟prediction error].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left[\underbrace{J_{t}^{\mathrm{exec},\omega}}_{\text{decision cost}}+\alpha\underbrace{\ell_{\mathrm{pred},t}^{\omega}(\widehat{d}_{t})}_{\text{prediction error}}\right]. (3.1)

We write ℒω​(θ)=𝒥ω​(θ)+α​ℒpredω​(θ)\mathcal{L}^{\omega}(\theta)=\mathcal{J}^{\omega}(\theta)+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}^{\omega}(\theta) for the loss of sample ω\omega, so that ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) is its mean over Ω\Omega. The nonnegative weight α\alpha controls the trade-off between decision cost and prediction error. The decision cost is the primary training objective. The prediction error anchors d^t\widehat{d}_{t} to observed demand. Figure 4 summarizes how forecasts affect execution through both LP decisions and reference construction, and contribute to training through the prediction loss.

3.2 Optimal-Basis Sensitivity

The computation graph combines explicit maps with implicit LP solution maps. The predictor and selectors can be differentiated directly. The initialization, pre-, and post-realization solutions require the sensitivity of an optimal LP solution to its inputs. The state fixes the initial stocks at each stage. Demand enters the request balances, and the post-realization LP fixes the current repositioning commitment gtexecg_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}. These inputs enter the RHS. The reference changes the constraint matrix, RHS, and objective coefficients through the affine movement equations (2.26) and the penalty terms in (2.30)–(2.31). Let init\mathrm{init} denote the initialization LP of Section 2.6, and let 𝒱LP={(0,init)}∪(𝒯×{pre,post})\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{LP}}=\{(0,\mathrm{init})\}\cup(\mathcal{T}\times\{\mathrm{pre},\mathrm{post}\}) collect the LP nodes. For each (t,σ)∈𝒱LP(t,\sigma)\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{LP}}, add nonnegative slack variables and let u~\widetilde{u} collect the physical and slack variables. Let c~tσ​(η)\widetilde{c}_{t}^{\sigma}(\eta), 𝖠~tσ​(η)\widetilde{\mathsf{A}}_{t}^{\sigma}(\eta), and 𝖻~tσ​(η)\widetilde{\mathsf{b}}_{t}^{\sigma}(\eta) denote the equality-form objective coefficients, constraint matrix, and RHS. (3.2)
Assumption 3.1 (Local optimal-basis stability).

At every LP node in 𝒱LP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{LP}} along the realized trajectory, there is a neighborhood of the full input vector in which the optimal solution is selected using the same basis index set and the associated basis matrix remains nonsingular.

Assumption 3.2 (Fixed branches).

Along the realized trajectory, there is a neighborhood of the inputs in which the repair rules in reference construction and the reallocation 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} each stay on the same branch, on which they are smooth.

Under Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, every map in the computation graph is locally differentiable, and the gradients derived below are exact. The first term follows the prediction-to-decision path of classical contextual optimization (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022): at fixed context, parameter changes alter the forecast and hence the decision. The second term is added by the multistage setting. It couples the stages: changes in the preceding optimal plan affect the current decision through the inherited state and reference construction. The third term is added by decision-dependent context. The inherited state depends on earlier decisions and also serves as prediction context, so changes in this state alter the forecast and then the current decision.

At stage zero, the state-gradient contributions vanish because 𝖩s,θ,0=0\mathsf{J}_{s,\theta,0}=0. 3.4 Multistage Forward and Adjoint Gradients

The fixed selectors Πz\Pi_{z} and Πs\Pi_{s} map the post-realization solution to the executed vector and next state in (2.39). The next stage also reuses the post plan through (2.41). Differentiating the selectors gives the forward recursion

𝖩z,θ,t:=∂zt∂θ=Πz​𝖩u,θ,tpost,\displaystyle\mathsf{J}_{z,\theta,t}:=\frac{\partial z_{t}}{\partial\theta}=\Pi_{z}\mathsf{J}_{u,\theta,t}^{\mathrm{post}}, 𝖩s,θ,t+1=Πs​𝖩u,θ,tpost,\displaystyle\mathsf{J}_{s,\theta,t+1}=\Pi_{s}\mathsf{J}_{u,\theta,t}^{\mathrm{post}}, ∀t∈𝒯.\displaystyle\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}. (3.14)

For trajectory ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega, combining the executed-cost and prediction-loss branches of (3.1) gives the forward gradient

∇θℒω(θ)=∑t∈𝒯[(𝖩z,θ,t)⊤c+α(𝖩d^,θ,t)⊤∇d^tℓpred,tω],∀ω∈Ω.\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{\omega}(\theta)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left[\left(\mathsf{J}_{z,\theta,t}\right)^{\top}c+\alpha\left(\mathsf{J}_{\widehat{d},\theta,t}\right)^{\top}\nabla_{\widehat{d}_{t}}\ell_{\mathrm{pred},t}^{\omega}\right],\qquad\forall\omega\in\Omega. The forward recursion propagates the total state–parameter Jacobian 𝖩s,θ,t\mathsf{J}_{s,\theta,t} and retains the preceding post-solution Jacobian at every stage. Because training needs only the gradient of a scalar objective, forming these full matrices is unnecessary. We therefore derive an adjoint recursion that computes the training gradient by propagating vector–Jacobian products backward through the computation graph. 4 Parallel Block Evaluation for Multistage Learning

The forward trajectory requires two LP solves per stage, in sequence, and training repeats it after every parameter update. These sequential solves take a large part of training time. We present parallel block evaluation, which accelerates the forward evaluation of the multistage policy. Nearby parameter values produce similar trajectories, so an earlier evaluation of the same sample gives approximate inputs for all stages. We first write the policy as a stage recursion and group contiguous stages into blocks (Section 4.1). The blocks are then evaluated in parallel, and repeatedly passing each block’s output to the next block restores the links between blocks (Section 4.2). An adjoint through all stages gives the training direction (Section 4.3). Section 4.4 gives the properties of the algorithm.

4.1 Stage Recursion and Block Maps

Successive stages depend on one another only through the preceding post optimal plan. This plan determines the next state and supplies the source plan for the next pre reference. We write ut=utpost,⋆u_{t}=u_{t}^{\mathrm{post},\star} for t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}. For fixed sample data, let FtF_{t} denote the prediction, reference construction, and commitment–recourse optimization at stage t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}. The first stage uses the given state s0s_{0} and the initialization LP, so u0=F0​(θ)u_{0}=F_{0}(\theta). Each later stage uses the preceding post plan, so ut=Ft​(ut−1,θ)u_{t}=F_{t}(u_{t-1};\theta) for t∈𝒯∖{0}t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{0\}. To expose parallel work, we partition the stages into MM contiguous blocks with boundary stages 0=t¯0<t¯1<⋯<t¯M=T0=\bar{t}_{0}<\bar{t}_{1}<\cdots<\bar{t}_{M}=T, where 1≤M≤T1\leq M\leq T. Block j∈ℳ:={0,…,M−1}j\in\mathcal{M}:=\{0,\ldots,M-1\} contains the stages 𝒮j={t¯j,…,t¯j+1−1}\mathcal{S}_{j}=\{\bar{t}_{j},\ldots,\bar{t}_{j+1}-1\}. The output of block jj carries the index j+1j+1 of the next block. Each block evaluates its stages exactly as serial evaluation does. Its block map ℱj=Ft¯j+1−1∘⋯∘Ft¯j\mathcal{F}_{j}=F_{\bar{t}_{j+1}-1}\circ\cdots\circ F_{\bar{t}_{j}} composes these stage maps in their original order and returns the last plan of the block.

4.2 Parallel Block Evaluation

We now solve the blocks in parallel. Under serial evaluation, block jj must wait for the last plan of block j−1j-1. The parameters change gradually during training. The trajectory of a sample therefore tends to stay close to the trajectory from its previous evaluation. That evaluation gives each block an approximate entry plan before the true one is known. All blocks can then be solved at the same time, as shown in Figure 6.

Block 00 starts from the given state s0s_{0}. For every other block j∈ℳ∖{0}j\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\{0\}, let u¯j\bar{u}_{j} be its entry plan. At first, u¯j\bar{u}_{j} is the candidate from the previous evaluation. Each block solves its stages in order. It returns its last plan u^j+1\widehat{u}_{j+1}:

u^1=ℱ0​(θ),u^j+1=ℱj​(u¯j,θ),∀j∈ℳ∖{0}.\widehat{u}_{1}=\mathcal{F}_{0}(\theta),\qquad\widehat{u}_{j+1}=\mathcal{F}_{j}(\bar{u}_{j};\theta),\qquad\forall j\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\{0\}. (4.1)

The candidates contain errors. The output u^j+1\widehat{u}_{j+1} generally differs from the entry u¯j+1\bar{u}_{j+1}. We therefore repeat the solve in passes. In each pass, the output of each block becomes the entry of the next block in the following pass (pass 2 in Figure 6). Let κ∈ℕ={1,2,…}\kappa\in\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\ldots\} index the passes. The parameters θ\theta stay fixed. We add the superscript (κ)(\kappa) to the entries and outputs of pass κ\kappa. Each pass applies (4.1) to the blocks it solves. The entries are updated by

u¯j+1(κ+1)=u^j+1(κ),∀j∈ℳ∖{M−1},κ∈ℕ.\bar{u}_{j+1}^{(\kappa+1)}=\widehat{u}_{j+1}^{(\kappa)},\qquad\forall j\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\{M-1\},\ \kappa\in\mathbb{N}. (4.2)

A block needs no new solve once its entry stops changing. Block 00 is solved only in pass 11. Block 11 has the same entry from pass 22 on. In general, block jj has the same entry from pass j+1j+1 on. We call block jj confirmed after its solve in pass j+1j+1. Pass κ\kappa thus solves only the blocks in ℳκ={j∈ℳ:j≥κ−1}\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}=\{j\in\mathcal{M}:j\geq\kappa-1\}. For a block j∉ℳκj\notin\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}, the output carries over from the previous pass: u^j+1(κ)=u^j+1(κ−1)\widehat{u}_{j+1}^{(\kappa)}=\widehat{u}_{j+1}^{(\kappa-1)}. Let KK denote the number of passes performed. The final records are the stage inputs, LP solutions, and optimal bases from the last solve of each block. Stages inside a block connect by construction. Mismatches appear only at block boundaries. The boundary residual after block j∈ℳ∖{M−1}j\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\{M-1\} in pass κ\kappa is rj(κ)=u¯j+1(κ)−u^j+1(κ)r_{j}^{(\kappa)}=\bar{u}_{j+1}^{(\kappa)}-\widehat{u}_{j+1}^{(\kappa)}. The stopping rule can end the passes after a fixed number of passes. It can also end them once the residuals of selected physical quantities fall below a preset threshold.

4.3 Training Direction from an Evaluated Trajectory

The backward pass runs on the final records of pass KK. Inside a block, each stage reads the output of the preceding stage. At the boundary after block jj, block j+1j+1 reads its entry u¯j+1(K)\bar{u}_{j+1}^{(K)}. This entry differs from the block output u^j+1(K)\widehat{u}_{j+1}^{(K)} by the residual rj(K)r_{j}^{(K)}. We hold these residuals fixed. Each entry u¯j+1(K)\bar{u}_{j+1}^{(K)} then equals the output u^j+1(K)\widehat{u}_{j+1}^{(K)} plus a constant. Its derivative with respect to that output is the identity. The adjoint recursion (3.16)–(3.19) therefore applies without change at the final records (Figure 7). Its parameter contributions give the training direction ∇~\widetilde{\nabla}. When all residuals vanish, ∇~\widetilde{\nabla} is the exact gradient. Otherwise, ∇~\widetilde{\nabla} is the gradient of the training loss with these residuals held fixed.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the forward passes and the backward pass for one training sample.

4.4 Algorithm Properties

Parallel block evaluation gains speed by stopping after a few passes, so its trajectory and training direction are approximate. Three questions then decide whether it can replace serial evaluation in training. First, do the passes reproduce the serial trajectory if they run long enough? If so, the algorithm approximates the serial policy rather than a different one. Second, how do the errors at the block entries change from pass to pass? The answer guides the choice of the number of blocks and passes. Third, how do these forward errors affect the training direction, which the parameter update uses? Proposition 4.1 answers the three questions. Let (utser)t∈𝒯(u_{t}^{\mathrm{ser}})_{t\in\mathcal{T}} denote the serial plans given by the stage recursion of Section 4.1.

Proposition 4.1 (Properties of parallel block evaluation).
  1. (i)

    Finite recovery. Suppose each stage map returns the same plan for the same inputs, independently of solver warm starts. Then at most MM passes reproduce the serial trajectory exactly.

  2. (ii)

    Error propagation. For t∈𝒯∖{0}t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{0\}, let LtL_{t} be a Lipschitz constant of FtF_{t}. In pass κ\kappa, the entry error of block jj is bounded by a multiple of the candidate error κ−1\kappa-1 blocks upstream:

    ‖u¯j(κ)−ut¯j−1ser‖≤(∏t=t¯j−κ+1t¯j−1Lt)​‖u¯j−κ+1(1)−ut¯j−κ+1−1ser‖,∀κ∈{1,…,K},j∈{κ,…,M−1}.\bigl\|\bar{u}_{j}^{(\kappa)}-u_{\bar{t}_{j}-1}^{\mathrm{ser}}\bigr\|\leq\Bigl(\prod_{t=\bar{t}_{j-\kappa+1}}^{\bar{t}_{j}-1}L_{t}\Bigr)\,\bigl\|\bar{u}_{j-\kappa+1}^{(1)}-u_{\bar{t}_{j-\kappa+1}-1}^{\mathrm{ser}}\bigr\|,\qquad\forall\kappa\in\{1,\ldots,K\},\ j\in\{\kappa,\ldots,M-1\}. (4.3)
  3. (iii)

    Gradient error. Suppose Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 hold between the final records and serial evaluation, and the stage maps and stage losses have bounded and Lipschitz first derivatives near the serial trajectory. Then the parallel training direction ∇~\widetilde{\nabla} and the exact serial gradient (3.15) satisfy

    ‖∇~−∇θℒω​(θ)‖≤Λ​maxj∈ℳ∖{0}​‖u¯j(K)−ut¯j−1ser‖,∀ω∈Ω.\bigl\|\widetilde{\nabla}-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{\omega}(\theta)\bigr\|\leq\Lambda\max_{j\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\{0\}}\bigl\|\bar{u}_{j}^{(K)}-u_{\bar{t}_{j}-1}^{\mathrm{ser}}\bigr\|,\qquad\forall\omega\in\Omega. (4.4)

Appendix E proves these statements. Part (i) answers the first question. Each pass confirms at least one more block, so the passes reproduce the serial trajectory for any partition into blocks. Recovery alone gives no speedup, however. The speedup comes from stopping after a few passes. Part (ii) answers the second question. Intuitively, an error in a candidate entry travels downstream by one block per pass, and each stage it crosses scales it by at most its Lipschitz constant LtL_{t}. When the product of the LtL_{t} over each block is below one, every pass shrinks the error that reaches a block, and a few passes suffice. When the product exceeds one, the error can grow, and more passes or shorter blocks are needed. Part (iii) answers the third question. The passes control only forward quantities, namely the plans at the block entries. Part (iii) shows that this suffices: the error of the training direction is at most a constant times the largest entry error in the last pass. Accurate entries therefore give an accurate training direction.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

The experiments use New York City ride-hailing trip data (New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission 2026). The city is partitioned into eight regions (Figure 8a), which gives 64 regional OD pairs. Requests are aggregated into five-minute counts. Appendix F.1 gives further details on the data and the model parameters. Repositioning is planned from 06:00 to 21:00 each day, which gives 180 decision stages. The data cover January 1 to April 30, 2026. January and February serve only as history for the forecasts. March (31 days) is used for training, April 1–10 for validation, and April 11–30 (20 days) for testing. All experiments share the same fleet, MFD curves, routes, background traffic, and daily initial states.

The multistage optimization uses five-minute periods, a 30-minute horizon (H=6H=6), and a waiting allowance Kwait=2K^{\mathrm{wait}}=2. The horizon covers a typical trip: passenger trips in March last 19 minutes on average. Most vehicles dispatched at a stage therefore finish their trips within the horizon, while the stage LPs stay small enough to be solved and differentiated many times in training. With the waiting allowance, a request can be served until the start of the second period after its arrival. Its patience is therefore 7.5 minutes on average. Costs and rewards are measured in US dollars. Waiting costs $0.67 per request-minute and repositioning costs $0.56 per committed mile (U.S. Department of Transportation 2025). We set the abandonment cost to $6.70, equivalent to ten minutes of waiting. Completion rewards use the January–February mean fare minus driver pay for each OD pair. The planning objective also contains the movement-error penalty, with weight cmfd=1,000c^{\mathrm{mfd}}=1{,}000, and the terminal cost, with ν=0.01\nu=0.01. LPs are solved with HiGHS 1.12.0 using dual simplex.

We evaluate all methods in an agent-based simulation of individual vehicles and requests. Every five minutes, a method decides from the aggregate state how many requests to serve, how many idle vehicles to reposition, and how many repositioning vehicles pick up en route. The simulation assigns these numbers to individual vehicles and recorded requests in the taxi zones of the city (Figures 8c and 8d), moves the vehicles at the regional MFD speeds, and returns the resulting state to the method at the next stage. The multistage performance of each method is therefore measured on the state of the simulated system rather than that of its planning model. Appendix F.2 describes the simulation. Validation, which selects the hyperparameters and checkpoints of every method, uses five-minute execution with one nonlinear MFD update per period. All test results in the main text come from the simulation.

5.2 MFD Optimization Model

We first examine the operational model itself. We compare the planning LP (2.32) with the fixed-fraction LP of Section 2.3 and measure the value of repositioning and pickup. These experiments use two demand forecasts. The historical-average (HA) forecast is the January–February mean by weekday, five-minute clock bin, and OD pair. The oracle uses the realized demand and removes forecast error. We report four operating metrics. Business benefit is the completion reward minus the waiting, abandonment, and repositioning costs, per request. Waiting time is the mean time from a request’s arrival to its match, its abandonment, or the end of the day. Abandonment and completions are percentages of requests. Table 1 reports the results on the 20 test days.

The planning LP outperforms the fixed-fraction LP with both forecasts. A more accurate forecast helps both planners: the oracle raises the benefit by 3.57% with the fixed-fraction LP and by 3.48% with the planning LP. Repositioning and en-route pickup add more. Without repositioning, the benefit falls by 12.16% with HA and by 14.29% with the oracle. Without pickup, it falls by 6.44% and 7.00%. This loss exceeds the direct value of the pickups: even if every pickup saved a request from abandonment, the pickups would explain at most a third of it. About half of the repositioning trips carry a passenger en route, so without pickups every repositioning trip runs empty, and the planning LP repositions about half as much (17,796 against 38,477 miles per day with HA). The reduced repositioning causes most of the loss through more waiting and abandonment.

5.3 Multistage Contextual Optimization

We next compare multistage contextual optimization (MCO) with the baselines in Table 2. All methods share the execution, the data splits, and the metrics. Their hyperparameters are tuned on the validation days and fixed before testing. Forecast root-mean-square error (RMSE) is measured in requests per OD pair and five-minute period, pooled over all horizon leads, stages, and days. We consider baselines from five paradigms, grouped as in the table. Appendix F.3 gives their implementation and training details.

Predict-then-optimize methods pass forecasts trained on prediction error to the same policy. They are MSE, our predictor (Appendix C) trained by mean squared error without state inputs; HA; STID, the spatial–temporal forecaster (Shao et al. 2022); ST-SSDL, which learns how demand deviates from its history (Gao et al. 2025); MAGE, which combines learned graphs of the OD pairs (Ma et al. 2025); and the oracle. Optimization under uncertainty replaces the forecast by historical demand scenarios (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020). SAA, CVaR, and RO minimize the mean, the conditional value-at-risk (Rockafellar and Uryasev 2000), and the worst case of the scenario costs, respectively. Heuristic rules use no optimization model. They give priority to service: idle vehicles first serve waiting requests, and a rule then repositions the remaining idle vehicles. Forecast-free rules use only the current state and recent requests: the +1 rule (Ruch et al. 2020), equal distribution (Gammelli et al. 2021), least-squares rebalancing (Valadkhani and Ramezani 2023), random walk (Guo et al. 2023), lost-request dispatch (Beojone et al. 2024), and real-time rebalancing (Pavone et al. 2012). Forecast-based rules set targets from a forecast: forecast-guided greedy dispatch with MSE forecasts (Guo et al. 2026); historical-share targets from HA; and target cruise toward the region with the highest MSE forecast (Guo et al. 2023). Among reinforcement learning (RL) methods, learned-value lookahead adds to the planning LP of MSE a value for each vehicle’s end region at the horizon, learned by temporal-difference learning (Wei et al. 2024, Huang et al. 2024b). End-to-end mean-field RL learns a policy that maps the operating state and demand features to repositioning shares by origin, trained by backpropagation through the five-minute model (Jusup et al. 2026). Atomic-PPO decides for small groups of idle vehicles in turn whether to serve, reposition, or stay, using one policy trained by proximal policy optimization (Dai et al. 2025). Finally, contextual optimization trains the predictor by decision cost. Per-stage zeroth-order adapts the per-stage training of Guo et al. (2026). It trains the predictor on the regret of each stage with a zeroth-order gradient estimate. MCO-serial evaluates each training day serially and uses the exact gradient, and MCO-parallel uses parallel block evaluation (Section 4). Appendix F.4 gives their training details.

MCO performs best in Table 2. It improves the benefit over MSE by 7.69% to 9.06% on all 20 test days, with the lowest waiting time and abandonment and the most completions, and MCO-parallel is slightly better than MCO-serial. Its forecasts are less accurate than those of MSE, so training on the decision cost trades accuracy for better decisions. More broadly, the methods that decide with an optimization model stay between −2.06%-2.06\% and +2.92%+2.92\% of MSE, whereas the heuristic rules lose 20% to 48% and mean-field RL and Atomic-PPO lose 22.89% and 35.49%, mainly through more abandonment. Among the optimization-based methods, how the predictor is trained matters more than its accuracy. STID and MAGE have the lowest RMSE but change the benefit by less than 1%, and per-stage zeroth-order, which trains each stage separately, loses 1.61%, so the effect of decisions on later states must enter training.

MCO also outperforms the oracle, which gains only 1.34%, so its gain does not come from accuracy. Exact demand is not the best input because the rolling-horizon policy is itself a heuristic for the multistage problem and the planning LP approximates the simulation with linearized MFD dynamics and aggregate flows. The oracle is therefore no upper bound for this policy. Because MCO trains the predictor on the cost of the executed decisions, it can learn forecasts that partly compensate for both gaps. MCO-parallel forecasts 9.0% above the demand, most for sparse OD pairs and before the morning peak. The policy then repositions 49% more vehicles than with MSE, also at midday, and loses 12.3% fewer requests, whereas the oracle repositions 6% more and loses 1.8% fewer.

5.4 Parallel Block Evaluation

This experiment measures how much parallel block evaluation speeds up training and whether its approximate gradient affects the quality of the trained model. We train MCO-serial and MCO-parallel for 30 epochs and evaluate both on the 10 validation days under five-minute execution at the end of each epoch. The validation benefit of both models rises over the epochs, and MCO-parallel is above MCO-serial in 24 of the 29 epochs after the first. The selected checkpoints gain 1.14% (MCO-parallel, epoch 26) and 1.08% (MCO-serial, epoch 29) on validation. In the simulation, MCO-parallel gains 9.06% on the test days and MCO-serial 7.69% (Table 2). The approximate gradient therefore does not reduce the quality of the trained model. The 30 epochs of training take 19.9 hours for MCO-parallel and 37.1 hours for MCO-serial, and at every epoch end of MCO-serial after the first, the most recent MCO-parallel checkpoint has the higher validation benefit. In the first epoch, MCO-parallel also evaluates every day serially. From the second epoch on, a visit to a training day takes about 75 seconds in MCO-parallel and 144 seconds in MCO-serial, a speedup of 1.91. The difference comes from the forward pass, which takes 38.5 seconds with parallel block evaluation and 104.4 seconds serially. The sequential backward pass takes 36.2 and 39.1 seconds.

5.5 Operational Insights

The results suggest four insights for platform operations. First, repositioning pays off most when the inherited fleet is far from demand. At 06:00, Manhattan South/Core and Brooklyn West/North generate 45.4% of the requests but hold only 10.3% of the idle vehicles. MCO-parallel repositions 3,521 vehicles in the first hour against 2,245 with MSE, and 90% of its reduction in abandoned requests falls before 15:00. Second, en-route pickup makes repositioning affordable. Without pickup, every repositioning trip runs empty, so the planning LP repositions about half as much and loses 6.44% of its benefit with HA. Third, the value of repositioning lies in its timing and destination rather than its volume. Most heuristic rules drive two to three times the repositioning miles of MSE per completed request, yet they lose 20% to 48% of the benefit. MCO-parallel, in contrast, saves about three abandoned requests per additional repositioned vehicle, mostly by moving vehicles from Manhattan South/Core, the two Queens regions, and Staten Island toward the two Brooklyn regions and the Bronx. Fourth, forecasts for repositioning should be judged by the decisions they produce. The most accurate forecasters change the benefit by less than 1%, and exact demand gains only 1.34%, whereas MCO-parallel gains 9.06% with forecasts 9.0% above demand.

6 Conclusion

This paper studied multistage contextual optimization for congestion-aware vehicle repositioning. We formulated a rolling commitment–recourse policy. It fixes repositioning before demand is realized and decides service afterward. A linearized MFD with a penalty on a movement-error bound keeps each stage an LP. We then trained the demand predictor on the decision cost of the whole multistage trajectory. The predictor uses the state left by earlier decisions as context. We derived the exact gradient and an equivalent adjoint that avoids full Jacobians. Finally, we proposed parallel block evaluation to speed up the sequential forward evaluation. It recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes. Its gradient error is bounded under early stopping.

In the New York City case study, evaluated in an agent-based simulation, multistage contextual optimization yields an additional 7.69% (MCO-serial) and 9.06% (MCO-parallel) of business benefit over the same predictor trained by mean squared error, on every test day. Both models also outperform the oracle forecast within the same policy. Exact demand therefore does not make this rolling, linearized policy optimal, and MCO learns forecasts that partly compensate for its gaps. For practice, the results suggest concentrating repositioning on the hours when demand moves away from the inherited fleet, letting repositioning vehicles pick up passengers en route, and judging forecasts by the decisions they produce rather than by their accuracy.

Several directions remain open. First, we treat demand as exogenous, but the distribution of vehicles also changes demand: short pickup times attract riders from other modes, so recorded requests depend on the policy that served them. Learning under such decision-dependent demand requires a model of how demand responds to supply. Second, we assume that vehicles follow the repositioning decisions. Human drivers choose where to go, so the platform must design incentives that make its decisions attractive to them. Third, platforms also control prices and matching, which interact with repositioning (Wang et al. 2025). Training a predictor on the joint cost of these decisions is a natural extension of multistage contextual optimization.

Transfers and completions follow (2.25), with fk,τaf^{a}_{k,\tau} given by (2.24); (2.18) then gives the idle and moving stocks at τ+1\tau+1, which is the next period’s initial state.

The procedure above constructs the reference for periods shared by the source plan and the current problem. The pre problem at stage t∈𝒯∖{0}t\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{0\} includes one additional period, t+H−1t+H-1, beyond the preceding post plan. We reuse that plan’s allocation shares from its final period t+H−2t+H-2 for the new period. Apply these shares to the new period’s propagated stocks and forecast using the rules above. Evaluate movement at that period’s own accumulation.

At the first stage, no preceding plan is available, so we obtain one by solving the fixed-fraction LP with s0s_{0} and d^0\widehat{d}_{0}. For each lead ℓ∈ℋ\ell\in\mathcal{H}, use this optimum’s corresponding quantities in (B.1). Starting from s0s_{0}, apply the repair and nonlinear propagation above under d^0\widehat{d}_{0}. Thus the fixed-fraction plan supplies the shares, while the endogenous MFD generates the reference stocks.

Appendix E Proofs for Parallel Block Evaluation

Proof of Proposition 4.1(i).

A block that starts from the serial plan solves the same LPs as serial evaluation. By the condition in part (i), it then selects the same solutions, so it reproduces serial evaluation and outputs the serial plan at its end. Block 00 starts from the given state s0s_{0}. Pass 11 therefore reproduces serial evaluation in block 00. By the update (4.2), the output of block 00 becomes the entry of block 11 in pass 22. This entry is the serial plan, so pass 22 reproduces serial evaluation in block 11. Its output becomes the entry of block 22 in pass 33, and so on. By induction, pass κ\kappa reproduces serial evaluation in block κ−1\kappa-1. Later passes do not solve this block again, so it keeps these serial records. After pass MM, all MM blocks hold serial records, and the final records reproduce the serial trajectory. ∎

Proof of Proposition 4.1(ii).

Let ej(κ)=‖u¯j(κ)−ut¯j−1ser‖e_{j}^{(\kappa)}=\|\bar{u}_{j}^{(\kappa)}-u_{\bar{t}_{j}-1}^{\mathrm{ser}}\| be the entry error of block jj in pass κ\kappa. For κ=1\kappa=1, the bound holds trivially because the product is empty and equals one. Fix κ∈{2,…,K}\kappa\in\{2,\ldots,K\} and j∈{κ,…,M−1}j\in\{\kappa,\ldots,M-1\}. By the update (4.2), the entry of block jj in pass κ\kappa is the output of block j−1j-1 in pass κ−1\kappa-1. The serial plan at the same stage is the output of the same block map at the serial entry. Hence

ej(κ)\displaystyle e_{j}^{(\kappa)} =‖ℱj−1​(u¯j−1(κ−1),θ)−ℱj−1​(ut¯j−1−1ser,θ)‖≤(∏t∈𝒮j−1Lt)​ej−1(κ−1)\displaystyle=\bigl\|\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\bigl(\bar{u}_{j-1}^{(\kappa-1)};\theta\bigr)-\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\bigl(u_{\bar{t}_{j-1}-1}^{\mathrm{ser}};\theta\bigr)\bigr\|\leq\Bigl(\prod_{t\in\mathcal{S}_{j-1}}L_{t}\Bigr)e_{j-1}^{(\kappa-1)} (E.1)
≤(∏t∈𝒮j−2∪𝒮j−1Lt)​ej−2(κ−2)≤⋯≤(∏t=t¯j−κ+1t¯j−1Lt)​ej−κ+1(1).\displaystyle\leq\Bigl(\prod_{t\in\mathcal{S}_{j-2}\cup\mathcal{S}_{j-1}}L_{t}\Bigr)e_{j-2}^{(\kappa-2)}\leq\cdots\leq\Bigl(\prod_{t=\bar{t}_{j-\kappa+1}}^{\bar{t}_{j}-1}L_{t}\Bigr)e_{j-\kappa+1}^{(1)}.

Each inequality holds because a block map composes Lipschitz stage maps, so it is Lipschitz with the product of their constants. Each step moves one block upstream and one pass back, until it reaches the candidate entry of pass 11. This is (4.3). ∎
