Appendix F Experimental Details

F.1 Data

The statistics below cover the 20 test days, 14 weekdays and 6 weekend days, between 06:00 and 21:00.

Demand. A test day has 493,625 requests on average, and the daily totals range from about 435,000 to 618,000. On weekdays, requests per five minutes reach a morning peak of 3,639 at 08:40 and an evening peak of 3,383 at 18:00. Weekends have no sharp morning peak and reach 3,607 at 20:00. Manhattan South/Core and Brooklyn West/North generate 45.4% of the requests (Figure 8a).

Fleet and initial states. The fleet of a day is set from the peak number of vehicles on trips on the same weekday in the previous eight weeks, and it is at least the number of vehicles on trips at 04:00. It averages 13,290 vehicles on the test days. At 04:00, the vehicles on trips are taken from the trip records and placed along their routes, no request is waiting, and the remaining vehicles are spread evenly over the regions. The five-minute model then runs without repositioning until 06:00 and gives the initial state of the day. At 06:00, the fleet is far from the demand: Manhattan South/Core and Brooklyn West/North hold only 10.3% of the idle vehicles, whereas the two Queens regions hold 50.2% (Figure 8b). This mismatch makes early repositioning valuable.

Traffic. Each region follows the speed MFD vk​(N)=vkf​(1−N/Nkjam)2v_{k}(N)=v^{\mathrm{f}}_{k}(1-N/N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}})^{2}, so its production is Pk​(N)=N​vk​(N)P_{k}(N)=Nv_{k}(N) and its critical accumulation is Nkjam/3N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}}/3. The free-flow speed vkfv^{\mathrm{f}}_{k} and NkjamN_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}} are fitted to the regional speeds and accumulations of March 2026 in 15-minute intervals (Table 3). The congested branch is rarely observed, so NkjamN_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}} is a fitted parameter rather than an observed jam accumulation. The background traffic Nk,τbgN^{\mathrm{bg}}_{k,\tau}, all vehicles other than ride-hailing, is reconstructed per region and 15-minute interval from county vehicle miles traveled, road traffic counts with their time profiles, and taxi and transit activity, and it is held constant within each 15 minutes. The platform accounts for 7.1% of the total accumulation on average.

Planning model parameters. The mean trip length ℓ¯k\bar{\ell}_{k} is the mean distance that a trip travels in region kk per regional movement, estimated from the March trip records along their region paths. With Δ=5\Delta=5 minutes, the movement fraction φk\varphi_{k} is largest at zero accumulation, where it equals Δ​vkf/ℓ¯k\Delta v^{\mathrm{f}}_{k}/\bar{\ell}_{k}. This value lies between 0.51 and 0.79, so φk<1\varphi_{k}<1 holds in every region. The envelope Ψ\Psi uses the points ξh\xi_{h} at 0, ±1\pm 1, ±5\pm 5, ±20\pm 20, ±100\pm 100, ±500\pm 500, ±2,000\pm 2{,}000, and ±10,000\pm 10{,}000 vehicles and at the endpoints ±maxk⁡Nkjam\pm\max_{k}N_{k}^{\mathrm{jam}}, which give S=16S=16 segments.

F.2 Agent-Based Simulation

The simulation runs from 06:00 to 21:00 and is not reset between stages. Each request appears at its recorded time at a point in its TLC taxi zone and abandons after a patience drawn uniformly between 5 and 10 minutes. The 262 zones are nested in the eight regions. A trip follows the region path of its OD pair, the same as in the planning model, along the shortest polyline through the transitions between consecutive regions, which are shared land borders, bridges, and tunnels. Passenger trips cover their recorded miles. Pickup legs and repositioning trips cover the straight-line and polyline distances, multiplied by detour factors fitted on the training days. Vehicles move in 15-second steps at the MFD speed of their current region, which depends on the accumulation of background traffic and fleet vehicles in that region. The zones are small, 1.2 square miles on average, so we do not add a within-zone control such as the coverage-based rebalancing of Zhu et al. (2024).

Every five minutes, the simulation receives the service, repositioning, and en-route pickup numbers of a policy and carries them out as hard limits in the order of the planning model. Fractional numbers are rounded by error diffusion, so the executed totals stay within half a unit of the planned totals over the day. Repositioned vehicles leave the zones of the origin region with the largest surplus of idle vehicles for the zones of the destination region with the largest shortfall. Every 60 seconds, en-route pickups come first: repositioning vehicles in a region are paired, closest pairs first, with waiting requests there whose destination is their target region. Service follows: waiting requests within the service number of their OD pair take, oldest first, the nearest idle vehicle of their region.

F.3 Implementation of the Compared Methods

All methods are trained on the 31 March days and observe the same information. In every period, the service is set at the start of the period from the waiting requests and the requests arriving in the period, and the simulation executes it as a hard limit. The LP-based methods commit their repositioning before the demand of the period is realized, whereas the rules reposition after serving when this demand is known. For the forecasters trained for accuracy, the learning rate is selected by the validation error of the forecast. All other hyperparameters and checkpoints are selected by the business benefit on the 10 validation days under five-minute execution. STID, ST-SSDL, and MAGE use the settings of their papers on the same data.

Optimization under uncertainty. At each stage, the five days of January to March whose OD demand in the last hour is closest to the current one provide five scenarios. The pre LP shares the current repositioning across scenarios, and the post LP shares the current service and pickup and plans later periods per scenario. CVaR averages the two worst of the five scenario costs.

Heuristic rules. Service favors the newest waiting requests, which raised the validation benefit of every rule. Each rule then sets a target number of idle vehicles for every region and moves a share of the gap to this target, with the share selected on the validation days. The +1 rule targets where recent requests started, equal distribution spreads the vehicles evenly, least-squares rebalancing matches them to the waiting requests, random walk spreads part of them over the adjacent regions, lost-request dispatch targets where requests were abandoned in the previous period, and real-time rebalancing evens them out together with the vehicles about to arrive. Forecast-guided greedy dispatch and historical share distribute them in proportion to the MSE and HA forecasts, and target cruise sends them to the nearby region with the highest forecast. Finally, repositioning vehicles pick up the remaining requests on their path whose destination is their target region.

Reinforcement learning. In learned-value lookahead, the value of a vehicle in a region at a given time is the completion reward of its next trip plus the discounted value at the destination and arrival time of that trip. It is learned by temporal-difference learning on rollouts of the training days and improved by one policy-iteration step. End-to-end mean-field RL serves by the rule of the heuristic methods and distributes the remaining idle vehicles with a multilayer perceptron, trained by backpropagating the business cost of whole days through the five-minute model. Atomic-PPO first imitates the decisions of MSE and is then trained by proximal policy optimization. Dai et al. (2025) designed it for 10 regions and about 300 vehicles. Our fleet has about 13,000 vehicles, so each decision unit is a group of vehicles.

Contextual optimization. Per-stage zeroth-order is not a reproduction of Guo et al. (2026), which trains STID forecasts against a rebalancing MILP, but keeps its two elements: a decision loss for each stage and a perturbation-based gradient estimate. With the state of a stage fixed, the forecast determines the repositioning, and the loss is the cost of the post LP under the realized demand with this repositioning. The gradient is estimated from one Gaussian perturbation of the forecast per stage. The method starts from MSE and uses the optimizer, prediction weight α\alpha, and number of epochs of MCO, so that the two differ only in the training signal.

F.4 Training of MCO

The MSE model has the architecture of Appendix C with the weights of the state inputs fixed at zero. MCO-serial and MCO-parallel start from it and learn the state weights during training. In the objective (3.1), ℓpred,t\ell_{\mathrm{pred},t} is the mean squared forecast error over the 6×646\times 64 horizon entries, normalized by the squared mean March OD demand per five-minute period. We set α=1,389.54\alpha=1{,}389.54, so that the weighted prediction loss of the MSE model equals 10% of the waiting, abandonment, and repositioning costs on two reference training days. A visit to a training day evaluates the day forward, computes the training direction with the adjoint, and makes one Adam update with learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. Both models are trained for 30 epochs, each visiting the 31 training days in the same random order. MCO-parallel uses M=16M=16 blocks, K=2K=2 passes, and eight workers. Its first visit to each day is evaluated serially, and later visits take their block entries from the previous visit to the same day.

The gradient is exact only in a neighborhood in which every LP keeps its optimal basis and every rule stays on its branch. Near a basis change, this neighborhood is very small, and the backward recursion over up to 180 stages can return a gradient orders of magnitude larger than usual. An update along such a gradient can raise the cost, and it inflates the step-size estimates of Adam for later updates. We therefore skip an update when its gradient is much larger than the recent ones. MCO-serial skips 35 of its 930 visits, and MCO-parallel skips 152.
